Microeconomics is the study of
• how households and firms make choices,
• how they interact in markets, and
• how the government attempts to influence
  their choices
Macroeconomics is the study of the economy
as a whole, including topics such as economic
growth, inflation, unemployment, and
macroeconomic policies.

  an economy's output
2. Apply the expenditure method for measuring
  GDP to analyze economic activity
3. Define and compute nominal GDP and real
  GDP
4. Discuss the relationships between GDP and
  economic well-being

         • Stock values and trends

• Systematic measurement of economic
  output developed during World War II

• Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is a measure
  of the productive capacity of an economy
• GDP also measures the total income of
  everyone in the economy
• And, it also measures total expenditure on the
  economy’s output of goods and services
• For the economy as a whole,
  income = expenditure, because every dollar of
  expenditure by a buyer is a dollar of income for
  the seller                                                                                                            4-9

• Illustrates GDP as spending, revenue,
  factor payments, and income.
• Factors of production are inputs like labor,
  land, capital, and natural resources.
• Factor payments are payments to the factors
  of production. (e.g., wages, rent)
• Households rent factors of production, buy
  and consume goods and services.
• Firms hire factors of production, produce
  goods and services                                                                                                           4-11

Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is

   The market value of

        Final goods and services

         Produced in a country in a given

• Aggregate measure of quantities produced
• More expensive items receive a higher
  weighting
  – Willingness to pay is an indication of benefit
     received from the good

• Orchardia's GDP is $64

 GDP
  – E.g. unpaid housekeeping and child care; self-
      fulfilled farmers
  – Measured GDP understates actual production
• Women's labor force participation has
  increased since 1960 (continue to work
  after marriage)
  – Working women's output is measured and

• Government goods and services are not sold in
  the market
   – E.g. national defense, public transportation,
     education provided by public
     schools, etc.
   – These goods have value
   – Increase overall output
   – Quantities are known
   – Prices cannot be established
• Government production is valued at cost
   – Overstates GDP if there is waste and inefficiency
   – Understates GDP if social value is greater than cost
                                                                                                     4-17
                                                                         17

• Final goods and services are consumed by the
  ultimate user
   – End products of production
   – Included in GDP
• Intermediate goods and services are used up in the
  production of final goods
   – Not included in GDP to avoid double counting
•  E.g. A baker pays $6 for flour and sugar for each box of
  doughnut
   – Baker charges $10 per box of doughnut
   – Doughnut adds $10 per box to GDP
   – Flour and sugar are not counted                                        4-18
                                                                           18

•  E.g. Milk can be sold as a final product or used as
  an intermediate good
   – Gallons of milk in the store
           • Consumed by households  final good
   – Gallons of milk sold to restaurants
           • Used to cook  intermediate good
• Intermediate goods are used up during the
  production of other goods
• Only final goods count towards GDP


                                                                                                    4-19
                                                                        19

• A capital good is a long-lived good used in the
  production of other goods and services
  not consumed final goods
   – Houses, apartments, and hotels
   – Stoves in restaurants, cooking schools
   – Delivery vehicles and taxis
•  Capital goods are not used up during production
  not intermediate goods
• Newly produced capital goods counts as Investment
   in that year
• Money (e.g. bank deposits and financial investments)
   is not a capital good                                                            4-20

a. The purchase of wheat from a wheat farmer by a

b. The purchase of an aircraft carrier by the federal

• Value added is the market value of the product minus
  the cost of inputs purchased from other firms
   – E.g. Grain is grown and harvested  grounded into flour 
     used with other ingredients to make bread
   – Sum of value added = the value of final goods and services
   – Count value added in the year it is produced  solve the
     problem that the production process may lasts across
      multiple years

An artist buys scrap metal from a local steel mill as a raw
material for her metal sculptures. Last year, she bought
$5,000 worth of the scrap metal. During the year, she
produced 10 metal sculptures that she sold for $800 each to
a local art store. The local art store sold all of the sculptures
at an average price of $1,000 each. For the 10 metal
sculptures, what was the total value added of the artist, and
what was the total value added of the local art store?

• "Domestic" in GDP means the activity is
  measured within a country's borders
  – Nationality of owners or company is not relevant
• Value must be produced in the year (time)
  considered
  – Sell a 20-year old house for $200,000
         • Pay $12,000 commission to the broker
         • Value added is $12,000
         • House was not produced in the period of time studied
         • Count income generated from the sale of used goods

George and John, stranded on an island, use clamshells
for money. Last year George caught 300 fish and 5 wild
boars. John grew 200 bunches of bananas. In the two-
person economy that George and John set up, fish sell for
1 clamshell each, boars sell for 10 clamshells each, and
bananas go for 5 clamshells a bunch. George paid John a
total of 30 clamshells for helping him to dig bait for fishing,
and he also purchased five of John’s mature banana trees
for 30 clamshells each. What is the GDP of George’s and
John’s island in terms of clamshells?

GDP is measured in three ways:
• Market value of production (from VAT
  accounts or firm survey of value added)
• Expenditure method
• Income method (tax reported household
  incomes)





                                                                                                  4-26
                                                                       26

• Four users of final goods
                      ■   Households     Firms
                      ■   Government     Foreigners
•  All goods produced are purchased by at least one
  of these groups in a given time period (year)
• Amount spent by the 4 sectors – spending on
  imports = market value of domestic production
• GDP can be measured in either way:
   – Market value of production
   – Total spending for final goods less value of imports

Consumption expenditure is spending by
households for goods and services
• Consumer durable goods are long-lived
  consumer goods
        • Cars         •  Furniture      •  Appliances
• Consumer non-durable goods are shorter-
  lived goods
        • Clothing         • Food           • Bedding
• Services are the largest component of
  consumer spending
        • Education     • Taxi rides       • Haircuts
                                                                                                 4-30
                                                                      30

Investment is spending by firms on final goods and services,
primarily capital goods.
•  Business fixed investment is purchases of new capital goods
      • Factories   • Office buildings   • Equipment
•  Residential investment is construction of new homes and
  apartment buildings  investment by the business sector
  which sells them to households
•  Inventory investment is the change in unsold goods to the
  company's inventory
   – These goods are produced but not yet sold
   – This entry can be positive or negative
            • Negative inventory investment means less in inventory at year-end than
             at the beginning
                                                                                                     4-31
                                                                         31

•  In period I, the manufacturer uses $10,000 of materials and
   supplies purchased and its own resources (such as labor) to
  produce the automobile  + $20,000 to inventory
•  In period II, the manufacturer ships the finished auto to an auto
   dealer. (Ignoring the shipping fee)
•  In period III, the dealer sells the auto to a consumer for $22,000.
  - $20,000 from inventory + $22,000 to consumption             4-32
                                                                            32

•  Residential Investment is the buying of newly
  constructed homes and apartments by Households
   – Real estate bought by firms for production is classed as
     business fixed investment
• Housing that is built and offered on the market, but
  not sold, are classed as Inventory Investment
   –  If sold in the next year, it is recorded as positive
      residential investment, and negative inventory investment
   – Dollar amount of inventory investment is estimated as
      asking price in the previous year
           •  If actual selling price is different, use a common price when
          deducting the inventory from Investment
                                                                                                    4-33
                                                                        33

•  Is it Double Counting?
   – Purchase of a house is investment
   – Living in a house is consumption (imputed rent)
• Consider: New capital goods contribute to both
  investment and consumption
   – Build a hotel (investment), rent out hotel rooms
     (consumption)
   – Build a shoe factory (investment), sell shoes
     (consumption)
•  Similarly, buying a newly built house is investment,
  renting it out (or staying in it) is consumption
   – Not double counting                                                                                                     4-34
                                                                         34

•  Financial investment
   – Purchases of stocks, bonds, and other financial assets
   – Purchase generally transfers ownership of a portion of
      the firm's existing capital stock or bonds
   – Similar to saving money in a bank or mutual fund
   – Does not correspond to any increase in physical capital
      or production capacity, in most cases
           • New stock issues can be an exception
• Economic investment: the increase in the capital
  goods used to produce other goods
   – This value is based on the market purchase price of the
      capital goods, not on company stock value
                                                                                                    4-35
                                                                        35

• Government purchases are final goods and
  services bought by federal, state, and local
  governments
     • Fighter jets      • Teaching       • Office supplies
• Excludes transfer payments
   – Transfer payments are made by government but the
     government receives no current goods or services
          • Social Security      Unemployment Insurance
        • No purchases of final goods and services
        involved in transfer payments
          – Spending by recipients is included in GDP
   – Transfer payments move wealth between households
• Excludes interest paid on government debt
                                                                                                  4-36
                                                                       36

Net exports equal exports minus imports
• Exports are goods and services produced
  domestically and sold abroad
   – Exports reduce the amount available to the domestic
    economy
• Imports are domestic purchases of goods and
  services produced abroad
   – Imports can be consumption, investment, or government
     spending
   – Imports increase the amount available to the domestic
    economy
   – Have to be subtracted from expenditure to estimate
     domestic production                                                         4-37
                                                                          37

• Terminology
  Y      Gross Domestic Product or output
  C      Consumption Expenditure
     I       Investment
  G     Government Purchases
  NX     Net Exports
• Expenditure approach to measuring GDP:

         Y = C + I + G + NX

• When a good is sold, its revenue is distributed to the
  workers or business owners involved in the production
• GDP = labor income + capital income
   – Measured before taxes
• Labor income is wages, salaries, benefits, and
  incomes of the self-employed
  – About ⅔ of GDP
•  Capital income is pays for physical capital (e.g.
   factories, machines) and intangible capital (e.g.
  copyrights, patents)
        • Profits for business owners    • Rent for land

• Compare GDP for different years to see
 how much output has changed
• However, GDP changes over time
  because
  – Prices change AND
  – Quantity of output changes
• To see how much output has grown,
  use only the changes in quantities
  – Hold prices constant
                                                                                                  4-44
                                                                       44

• GDP in 2009 is $175; GDP in 2013 is $420
  – GDP in 2013 is 2.4 times the GDP in 2009
• Only twice as many pizzas and pies were
  produced in 2013
  – Market value of output grew faster than the
     physical volume of output
          Number of    Price of   Number of    Price of
              Pizzas       Pizza        Pies        Pies
  2009      10       $10       15       $5
  2013      20       $12       30       $6
                                                                                                  4-45

• Real GDP values output in the current
  year using the prices from the base year
  – The base year is a reference year that
    changes infrequently
  – Real GDP measures the real physical volume
     of production
• Nominal GDP values output in the current
  year using prices from the current year
  – Nominal GDP is the current dollar value of
     production                                                                    4-46
                                                                       46

• Use 2009 as the base year
• Nominal GDP for 2009 is $175 and for 2013, $420
• Calculate real GDP using current year quantities
  and base year prices
   – Real GDP in 2013 is
         (20 pizzas) ($10) + (30 calzones) (5) = $350
          • Real GDP doubled between 2009 and 2013

          Number of    Price of   Number of    Price of
               Pizzas       Pizza        Pies        Pies
   2009        10         $10         15         $5
   2013        20         $12         30         $6

                                                                                                           4-50
                                                                             50

•  Usually, nominal and real GDP increase each year
• Sometimes, during a recession, both nominal and real
  GDP decrease
• Nominal GDP can go up and real GDP go down
   – Fewer goods and services produced AND
   – Prices increase faster than output decreased
• Nominal GDP will be smaller than real GDP if the prices in
  the current year are less than in the base year
   – Usually true for years before the base year
•  Real GDP could rise and nominal GDP fall, but this is rare
   – Prices are falling faster than output is increasing
                                                                                                      4-51
                                                                          51

a.  “If nominal GDP is less than real GDP in a given year,
   then the price level must have fallen this year compared
    to the base year.”


b. “Whenever real GDP declines, nominal GDP must also
    decline.”

c.  “If a recession is so severe that the price level declines,
   then we know that both real GDP and nominal GDP
   could decline.”



                                                                                                      4-52
                                                                          52

• Real GDP per capita (income per person)
  is a flawed measure of well-being
  – Ignores leisure, environment and non-
     material quality of life
  – It values only market transactions
  – Ignores poverty and economic inequality





                                                                                                      4-53
                                                                          53

• Amount of leisure time has increased in the
  past 100 years
  – Work weeks are shorter
  – People enter the labor force at an older age
• Leisure produces no goods for market
  – GDP places a value of zero on all leisure time
  – Opportunity cost of an hour of leisure is your
     hourly wage
  – Omission of the value of leisure time makes
   GDP seem smaller
                                                                                                    4-54
                                                                        54

• GDP omits services that are not traded in
  markets
  – household production
  – volunteer services
  – illegal transactions
• Valuing these services would be difficult
• Nonmarket activities are important in poor
  countries
  – Many self-sufficient households and bartered
    goods and services                                                                                                      4-55
                                                                          55

• Underground economy (“black market”) is all
  unreported transactions, legal and illegal
• Casual labor is often paid in cash
   – Failure to report transaction reduces taxes
   – Includes baby sitters, lawn care, home repair, etc.
• Some underground activity is illegal
   – A service of value is provided
   – Drug dealers, fences, prostitution, etc
• Estimates suggest the underground economy is
  large regardless of national income level

                                                                                                    4-56
                                                                        56

• Suppose a factory is built in your town
  – People are employed and output is produced
         • Productive activity is included in GDP
• Suppose further that the factory creates
  pollution
  – Your city hires a company to restore the
    environment to its initial condition
  – Clean-up activities are included in GDP
         • Gets environment back to its starting point, not better
         • Overstates economic production
                                                                                                     4-57
                                                                         57

• No adjustment is made for the decline in
  resource availability when mining or other
  harvesting is done
  – One more barrel of oil on the market means one
     less barrel for future use
• Environmental quality and resource depletion
  are difficult to value
  – They have value but is omitted from GDP
• Environmentalist critique of economics:
  – Economic development sacrifices future
     generations for present well-being
                                                                                                     4-58
                                                                         58

• GDP does not capture the effects of income inequality
   – Inequality can lower median income
   – Most would prefer living in a relatively equal society to one
      with a few wealthy and many poor
•  Inequality worsens many social indicators:
   – Social cohesion & crime rates
   – Self-reported happiness & life satisfaction
   – Mental illness, physical health & longevity
•  Inequality has been increasing for the last 30 years in
  most developed countries
   – Inequality is especially high in the US and in HK
                                                                                                        4-60
                                                                           60

• GDP does not account for intangibles people value
   – Crime rates
   – Traffic congestion
   – Civic organizations
   – Sense of community
• Maximizing GDP will not necessarily maximize national
  well-being
   – Whether increases in output increase welfare is a case-by-
     case issue
   – Other quality of life measures:
           • UN’s Human Development Index
           •  Quality-of-life Index
           • Gross National Happiness
                                                                                                      4-61
                                                                          61

• Real GDP per capita is often used to measure the
  standard of living in a country
• GDP per capita is observed to be positively associated
  with several measures of well-being
   – Material standard of living: more goods and services
   – Health and life expectancy
         • Residents of high income countries have fewer of
        health problems and live longer
   – Education
         • Literacy and school enrollment rates are higher in
        high-income countries
